en: The Therī-apadāna,
Chapter on the Khattiyās:
The Apadāna of the Eighteen Thousand Bhikkhunīs Headed by Yasavatī.
“All existences are completely exhausted;
existence has been stilled and liberated.
And for us, all taints no longer exist.”
We announce it, O Great Sage:
whatever wholesome karma was previously performed that was well-directed.
This offering consisting of enjoyments is given for your sake, O Great Sage,
for the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas.
And the desired gift of enjoyment was given for your sake, O Great Sage.
This karma consisting of high and low,
well-undertaken by the bhikkhus,
results in rebirth in a high-born family.
What is this, O Great Sage?
Impelled by that very root of merit,
the perfection of karma has been activated.
Transcending the human state,
they were born into a family of kṣatriyas;
and when the work was accomplished, they arose.
Or even from the same caste;
those born together in the later period were Kṣatriyas born of noble lineage.
Possessing beauty, possessing wealth,
honored with gain, honor, and reverence—
within the inner palace, O Great Hero.
Like the gods in the Nandana grove.
Having become disenchanted with the household life,
I went forth from home into homelessness.
For some days now,
we have all attained Nibbāna.
[We have renounced] robes and almsfood...
They bring us many requisites for bedding and seating;
we are always honored and worshipped.
The defilements have been incinerated by us;
all states of existence have been utterly uprooted;
like a nāga who has severed its bonds, we are free.
We dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to us in the presence of my Buddha.
The three true knowledges have been attained;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical insights—
And these eight liberations have been realized; the six direct knowledges have been attained;
the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.”
Thus indeed, eighteen thousand noble women who were bhikkhunīs, headed by Yasavatī, recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One.
This is the first account of the eighteen thousand bhikkhunīs headed by Yasavatī.
